quotes.text: Routing decides where a request should go, and the firewall decides whether it should be allowed through at all. It inspects the whole request, including the headers and the body.

quotes.text: The practical effect is that a dead server drops out of rotation and comes back by itself. Nobody has to sit there and babysit it at three in the morning.

quotes.text: Your servers stop spending effort on cryptography and get to focus on your application. You also manage certificates in one place instead of chasing them across every machine in the pool.

quotes.text: Microsoft recommends running a new firewall in detection mode for a short while in production. That way, you can spot false alarms and tune them out before you start blocking real traffic.

takeaways: Azure Application Gateway is a regional layer 7 load balancer that reads the URL path and host name, so it can route images, video or whole websites to different back-end pools.
Health probes keep dead servers out of rotation automatically, and TLS termination at the gateway takes encryption work off the servers and keeps certificates in one place.

The WAF v2 tier blocks attacks like SQL injection and cross-site scripting using OWASP-based rules, and Application Gateway is often combined with Azure Front Door or Azure Load Balancer rather than chosen instead of them.
hook: Most load balancers never read the requests they deliver, which is why routing, encryption and attack protection often end up scattered across your servers. This episode is for cloud beginners, developers and IT pros who keep seeing Azure Application Gateway in architecture diagrams. You will understand listeners, routing rules, health probes, TLS termination, the web application firewall and how it compares to the other Azure load balancers.
